open.description: prism: faces left out at the back, so the rooms inside show; with piers, any number opens the core's whole back, the piers there left closed

panels.description: shape: its straight sides as tiles on bricks with side studs every other course (true, the default), or plain bricks (false).

pattern.description: repeat: the bricks again, stepped each time. mirror: everything so far, reflected about a line — build one side and mirror it rather than writing both. fill: a footprint tiled with the largest plates that fit, or with rise 3 a wall of short bricks in a running bond — and with layers, a shrink and a wall it is a dome, a cone, a hull, a tube or a bowl in one object. rock: a crag in one object — courses stepping in unevenly towards a peak off the middle, faced with slopes, cheese slopes, pebbles and bare ledges in two greys; a different seed is a different rock. studs_out: a face built sideways in one object — courses of 1x1 bricks with a side stud, tied by plates, each stud carrying a tile, round tile, round plate or cheese slope laid on its side; the arithmetic of where a side stud is, done for you. prism: a many-sided shaft in one object — a tower, a pier, a turret of 5 to 16 sides, each face a bonded wall turned to its angle about the middle (at is the middle), grooved where the faces meet. round: anything round in section, in one object — a column, a rocket stage, a lighthouse, a silo, a boiler, a fuselage, a tree trunk — of the round parts sets use at each diameter (round bricks, cylinder halves, corner rounds tied by round plates), colour bands, cones, Technic struts and spokes up its stack, ending in a nose; upright or lying along x or z. shape: a body that is not a box, said as solids — a loft through cross-sections, an extruded side profile, a revolve, a box with rounded or cut corners and edges, an ellipsoid or dome — less any cuts, laid in the parts a builder would choose: bricks and plates inside, slopes and curved slopes fitted to the surface's fall, inverted slopes under it, wedge plates on a diagonal edge, round parts where a section is round, a side that curves up and down laid on its side on side studs, tiles on top, one half and its mirror; a car's body, a hull, a fuselage, an animal's body. Another shape standing on it keeps its studs there. shell: a dome or a ball bigger than a dish, in one object — twelve strips of flat panels on clip hinges round a ring, each band's panels sized to its round, the strips taking turns low and high so the high ones lap the low ones' edges, tapered with wedge plates, each band lapping the one above, under a dish; a ball hangs the same strips under the ring on a stand. Its bands are sections ("shell 3.2": strip 3, band 2) an edit can turn or repaint. figure: a character in one object, built as a set builds one — a person, a four-legged animal or a head on a neck, every limb, the head and the tail on a working joint (ball shoulders, a turning or ball neck, a tail on a bar), posed by words, sized and coloured as said, its parts named to build on and pose again.

piers.description: prism: faceted piers clustered round it, each a prism of its own built against the core, with a cleft between each two — a tower like Orthanc in one object. The core is capped with a summit two plates thick at y + 3 x courses, and piers taller than the core rise past it as horns: blades of plates on their side, cut by wedge plates, sweeping out and back in to a point (the reply says where the tips are).

courses.description: how tall, in courses of three plates; more than the core's for horns (a fifth more; a blade rises at least two and a half times its width)

flare.description: blade: studs its sweep reaches out (half its width)

horns.description: what piers taller than the core rise into: a blade (the default, as set 10237 builds Orthanc's), a square spire stepping in to a point, or flat, a turret's cap

out.description: studs from the core's middle to each pier's (set into the core by its wall's thickness)

radius.description: studs from a pier's middle to the outside of its faces (two thirds of the core's; smaller than keeps faces two studs wide at its sides, it is laid at that and said)

turn.description: degrees round from +z to the first pier (between two faces, so there is a cleft front and back)

plinth.description: prism: {"steps": 1 to 4, "out": studs, "stair": true, "rock": true} — the tower raised on square terraces stepping down from its foot, two courses each, their tops tiled in the second tone up to its faces, with a stair cut into the front (+z) up to its door's level, and crags in its dark tones rising against it at their corners and sides (rock: false for none). The reply says the tower's foot (and add_rooms' y).

pose.description: figure: {"right arm" and "left arm": down, bent, forward, raised, out, or [[out, up, forward] of the upper arm, the same of the forearm]; "seated": true sits a person on a seat of its own; "head": degrees it turns (an animal's: up, down, forward, left, right); "tail": raised, level, down}

radius.description: prism: studs from the middle to the outside of a face

revolve.description: shape: {"axis": "y", "x" or "z", "centre": [x, y, z], "profile": [[along it (plates up y, studs along x or z), radius in studs], ...]}; along x or z, "screen" as on an extrude.

rise.description: fill: plates between layers. 1 for plates, which is the default; 3 for courses of bricks.

seed.description: rock: which rock — each number leans and wanders its own way

shrink.description: fill: studs off each layer, taken half from each side, so the stack tapers as it rises. Must be even. 2 is a dome, 4 a steep cone, 0 a straight-sided hull, and -2 flares outward.

sideways.description: fill, prism: the share of its 1x2 bricks laid as two 1x1 bricks with a stud on the side, turned out and dressed with a tile, round tile, round plate or cheese slope on that stud, 0 to 0.5. For a wall one stud thick: a face built partly on its side, as real sets build them.

solids.description: shape: what it is made of, each an object naming one kind — {"loft": {...}}, {"extrude": {...}}, {"revolve": {...}}, {"box": {...}}, {"ellipsoid": {...}} or {"dome": {...}} — with its own "color" if it wants one (the last that holds a stud gives it its colour). Studs across and along, plates up, from at.

stack.description: round: what goes up the axis, bottom first, each square on the last. {"plates": N} a length of body ("color" a band of another colour, "diameter" wider or narrower, "spokes": 4 or 2 its top plate reaching a stud out with a "tile" on each reach — grid fins, gallery brackets, yard stubs); {"cones": 9 or 1} cones under a round plate ("cone_color") — nozzles, engine bells, lamps; {"technic": true, "struts": 0-4} a course with a pin hole out of each side and a Technic beam pinned on that many sides ("strut_color", "strut_length" in holes) — legs, stays; {"nose": cone, ogive, dome, point or flat} its top, and the end of the stack.

step.description: repeat: how far each copy moves, in studs and plates

storeys.description: prism: {"count": 2 to 8, "in": studs} — the courses split into storeys, each in studs smaller than the one below (its piers drawn in with it) and standing on a ledge two plates thick in the second tone, only the top storey's piers rising into horns: a tower that steps in as it rises, not a shaft. The reply says the top's radius (for add_rooms) and its summit's y.

surface.description: shape: curved slopes on its surface or straight ones; auto (the default) is curved if any solid is rounded.

thickness.description: prism: 2 (the default) closes the inside; 1 leaves slits at the corners

top.description: shape: tiles over its top (the default) or studs left showing.

top_color.description: shape: the colour of its top tiles and slopes, if not its own.

wall.description: fill: leave the middle out, this many studs in from every side. An ellipse with wall 1 is a round tube; a rectangle with wall 1 is a room's walls.

wheels.description: shape: a car on its own wheels — studs along x of each axle's middle, under a body laid along x 6, 8, 10 or 12 studs across. Each axle is a wheel and tyre each side on a Technic axle through Technic bricks, on a chassis of plates under them from nose to tail; the body cut clear of each wheel's box stands on the bricks (its underside 5 plates up or lower over them) and the chassis, so the car is one piece on its wheels. wheel_color is the rims' colour.

window_color.description: prism: the windows' colour (40, Trans-Brown, a dark slit, unless said)

windows.description: prism: a few narrow windows up every other face, a storey apart, dark slits unless window_color says; none unless said

around.description: {"x", "z"}: a centre, in the coordinates the section is built in. Each copy is carried round it by its yaw step, keeping its pitch and roll — a ring of panels round a dome.

axis.description: which way that pin runs. Defaults to the source section's.

degrees.description: turned this much further per copy, about the section's own origin. Put that origin at the centre of a tower and this walks the copies round it.

from.description: the name of a section that already has bricks in it

name.description: what to call the copies. They are numbered from 2.

times.description: how many copies to make, each one step further than the last

yaw.description: degrees further round per copy (360 / how many in the ring)

axis.description: or one turn about one pin: z tips it left and right, x forward and back, y swings it round. Applied after yaw, pitch and roll.

degrees.description: how far it is turned about that axis or line. Any angle.

hinge.description: turn it on a real joint, both halves laid for you: "tilting" (or true; 3937 under 3938, rests closed), "clip" (60478's bar in 63868's clip, rests in line), "click" (44302/44301, in line, where this build's parts have it). x, y, z are then where the base stands, like any brick, turned by yaw about its first stud; the section's bricks start at 0,0,0 on the top half's studs, its nose (+z) running away from the joint's line, and pitch lifts it about that line (or roll, with the line along z). A section that leans must turn on a joint; this is the one-line way.

line.description: or the turn's axis as a direction [x, y, z], instead of axis

name.description: what to call it, e.g. port nacelle

pitch.description: then degrees its nose lifts. Yaw and pitch together face a panel any way round a dome and tip it to the curve.

within.description: the section this one is built in: x, y, z (and its hinge's base) are then that section's own coordinates, and it goes where it goes. Panels hinged on panels, a chain round a dome.

x.description: studs across, where this section's own origin sits

yaw.description: degrees about the upright: its +z (its nose) swings towards +x. Applied first.

sketch.description: true for a sketch: massing only, under 150 parts, checked and pictured but not built. Three are made to choose between before the full design, each a different idea: in silhouette, proportion or approach.

name: submit_design

description: Stand a minifigure in the model, made from real parts in their real places: who lives in it, guards it, works in it — or the subject itself, where the brief asks for a person at minifigure scale (a pilot, a knight on a horse). Add them once what they stand on is built — submitting a whole new design replaces them. Each slot takes a part number or a few words matched against the names of the parts made for it ("wizard hat", "long beard", "robe", "staff"); leave a slot out for a plain one. It stands on whatever is highest under its feet, two studs side by side, and is refused if something is in the way. Its parts are not counted in the model's variety, as a set's figures are not.

accessory.description: what it holds in its right hand

accessory_left.description: what it holds in its left hand

arms.description: plain, printed sleeves, or another arm ("skeleton", "wing")

back.description: airtanks, a backpack, a quiver, wings, or left out

colors.description: LDraw colour codes by slot: headwear, hat_extra, head, neck, back, cape, torso, arms, hands, hips, hipwear, legs, footwear, accessory, accessory_left. A printed torso brings arm and hand colours of its own.

facing.description: which way its face looks: +z, the default, is towards the front view

footwear.description: flippers, skis, skates, or left out

hands.description: plain, or a hook, boxing gloves, a prosthetic

hat_extra.description: a visor, plume or feathers fixed onto the headgear

hips.description: a printed belt or sash, or left out

hipwear.description: a skirt, a tail or a belt over the hips

legs.description: plain, printed, "short" for a child, a wooden leg, a mermaid tail

name.description: who it is; the name of its sub-model in the saved file

neck.description: armour, a scarf, a beard, a life jacket, or left out

torso.description: what is printed on the chest; an odd body (a battle droid, a skeleton) brings its own head, arms and legs

x.description: studs: the first of the two studs it stands on

y.description: plates: the height of the floor it stands on, which a room or a balcony with anything over it needs; left out, it stands on whatever is highest at that spot

name: add_minifig

description: Make a part the LEGO Group has not made, when no real part will do: search_parts first, and use a real one if there is one. Either a new part of a family at any size — a 1 x 7 brick, a bracket with a 3 x 2 upright, a Technic brick 1 x 9, a brick with studs on two sides — or a real part changed: from="3700" with across 6, from="3062b" without its studs, from="3003" with a corner cut out. It is checked as a person's part is (sizes the system has, walls 1.6 mm, studs on the grid) and refused with the reason if it cannot be made. Made, it is a part like any other: put its number in check_design, edit_model or submit_design, and a saved model carries it. Its studs, holes and pins are found as a real part's are, so it clutches and pins as they do.

across.description: studs along X: a brick's length; a slope's, bracket's or curved slope's width along its face or upright; a Technic brick's length. With from: the new length.

angle.description: slope, inverted: one of the named angles of LEGO® slopes, which sets run and plates as the real part has them

cut.description: with from: a box to cut out of the part — a corner, a notch, a step — in studs from its low x and low z (its left and back) and plates up from its bottom; the cut faces are closed and a wall put back where it opens the part's hollow underside.

deep.description: studs along Z: a brick's width; a slope's depth from back to foot; a bracket's plate depth. With from: the new width.

family.description: for a new part: brick (also plates and tiles: plates 1, studs false), slope, curved (a curved slope), inverted (slope), round, bracket (a plate with an upright whose studs face forward), technic (a 1 x N brick with a hole between every two studs)

from.description: instead of a family: a real part's number to change, keeping everything not changed as the LEGO Group made it. Longer, wider and taller repeat a slice of it; a part with no slice that repeats (a 1 x 1, a round brick across) is refused.

name.description: what to call it; left out, it is named as LDraw names its parts

plates.description: height in plates, 3 to a brick (a bracket is 1, a Technic brick 3). With from: the new height.

rise.description: bracket: the upright's height in studs

run.description: slope, inverted, curved: the rows the face falls over, from the front; the rest are flat with studs

sides.description: brick: the sides with studs on them, letters of fblr: f is the +z face (the front), b -z, l -x, r +x; studs 10 LDU under the top and every stud down. Needs 3 plates or more.

studs.description: a new part: true for studs on top (the default), false for a tile. With from: "keep", "none" to take them off, "fill" to put them on wherever the top is flat.

way.description: bracket: whether the upright hangs down from the plate's front edge or stands up from it

name: make_part

annotations.title: Lay a picture as Brick Art

description:
Lay a picture as a LEGO® Art set is laid — 31212 The Milky Way, 31208 The Great Wave, 31213 Mona Lisa — on 16 x 16 panels joined underneath into one piece: square tiles merged where it is flat, 1 x 1 round tiles for texture, quarter circles along curved contours, stars in trans-clear, glow-in-the-dark, pearl and metallic set a plate proud, and the subject raised on stacked plates with cheese slopes. Use this, not submit_design, whenever a mosaic, a picture in bricks, wall art or something like a LEGO® Art set is asked for. It replaces what is on the baseplate.
The picture is the one the person chose (look_at_picture shows it). With none, draw it yourself as svg: one stud is one pixel, so big simple shapes in flat colours, like a poster.
You decide what a designer of LEGO® Art sets decides, and the app reads everything you leave out off the picture: the panels and the crop; regions over the picture, each with its texture, its relief (the subject raised, the background flat), whether contours run in it and whether its points of light are stars and in what finish; single stars put exactly where you want them; a palette to keep to. Coordinates are fractions of the picture, 0 to 1 from its top left. Later regions lie over earlier ones and change only what they say, so start with the whole picture and work inward. A plan that cannot be laid is refused with every fault named.
The answer is the picture as laid, face on, and what it is made of. Look at it as a person would from across a room, and call make_art again with the plan changed if it does not read as the subject.

base_colour.description: the panels' LDraw colour, which shows between round tiles: usually the darkest of the background

depth.description: how high relief read off the picture rises where no region gives one; 0 keeps it flat there. Default 3.

name.description: the picture's title

palette.description: LDraw colour codes to lay it in, as a set keeps to a dozen or so. Leave it out for all of them.

panels.description: [across, down], 1 to 6 each; a panel is 16 studs, 12.8 cm. down 0 keeps the picture's proportions. A large set is 4 to 6 across.

points.description: single stars put by hand (default 1 x 1 trans-clear). A sky like 31212's has dozens, of varied size and finish

at.description: [x, y], fractions of the picture from its top left

finish.description: a star's finish: trans-clear, glow, pearl-white, pearl-grey, pearl-gold, metallic-gold, metallic-silver, trans-light-blue, trans-medium-blue, trans-dark-blue, trans-yellow, trans-orange, trans-red, trans-purple, or an LDraw colour code

size.description: 1 (default): a 1 x 1 round tile; 2: a 2 x 2 round tile, for the few brightest

colour.description: lay the whole region in this one LDraw colour, whatever the picture has there

contours.description: curved edges inside it laid in quarter-circle tiles (default true)

rx.description: half-width, a fraction of the picture's width

ry.description: half-height, also a fraction of the WIDTH, so rx = ry is a circle

everything.description: the whole picture; put it first

finish.description: a star's finish: trans-clear, glow, pearl-white, pearl-grey, pearl-gold, metallic-gold, metallic-silver, trans-light-blue, trans-medium-blue, trans-dark-blue, trans-yellow, trans-orange, trans-red, trans-purple, or an LDraw colour code

name.description: what it is: sky, core, the crest

items.description: [x, y], fractions of the picture from its top left

relief.description: plates it stands above the panel. The background 0; the subject raised in terraces, an outer region 1 and an inner 2 or 3; cheese slopes are laid on the way up

stars.description: whether points of light the picture has here become stars in a finish (default true). False on a subject whose highlights are not stars

texture.description: round: 1 x 1 round tiles, the theme's texture, for what is busy or soft (a star field, foam, cloud, hair, fur); smooth: square tiles merged into long ones, for flat colour (sky, a wall, a plain ground); picture: round where the picture is busy and smooth where it is flat

svg.description: the picture, drawn, when the person has not chosen one: a whole <svg> with a viewBox in the panels' proportions (0 0 96 48 for 6 x 3 panels, a unit a stud) and a rect filling it as the background. Leave it out to use their picture.

name: make_art

description: The picture the person chose to make into Brick Art, as they gave it, with its size in pixels. Look at it before writing a make_art plan from it. When there is none it says so: draw one in make_art's svg.
name: look_at_picture

description: What the person has selected in Brickworks — the parts they mean by "this", "these" or "the selected": each by number with where it stands, their box, the sub-assembly they are in, the room a change about them may use, how the joints round them stand, and pictures with them picked out, close up and in the whole model. Call it whenever a request is about part of the model, then change that part with edit_selection.
name: selection

description: Change the selected parts as edit_model does — take off, paint, move, put down — keeping to the selection's room: a change that reaches outside it is refused whole, and everything else in the model stays where it is. It is checked as any design is, so a change that would not hold together or leaves a part loose changes nothing, and the refusal says, part by part, what each ran into or why nothing holds it, and the nearest place it fits and holds. check_only=true tries a change without making it. Other copies of the sub-assembly follow the change. One undo takes the request back. For more room, give room= and why=: the person is asked first.

attach.description: put it on another part connector to connector, instead of x, y, z, face and rot: the app works out the pose and seats it exactly, at any angle the joint turns to. How figures and small models are built: legs on hips, an arm on a shoulder, a hand on the arm, a wing on a hinge, a tail on a bar, a head on a neck. show_technique "posed minifigure" or "limb on a clip" is one written out; attachment_points lists a part's connectors.

align.description: [a direction of this part, one of the model's]: turn it about the joint until the first lies along the second, as ["+z", "up"] or [[0, 0, 1], [0, 1, 0]], then yaw from there. On a ball it points that way whatever the ball's axis: ["-x", [0.94, -0.34, 0]] is out along x and 20 degrees down

by.description: this part's own connector that goes there, as "hinge[0]"; leave out when only one fits

flip.description: an axle, bar or hinge joint the other way round, end for end

orient.description: this part's whole turn in the model, as a section's yaw, pitch and roll: a ball takes any; a hinge, clip or axle only one that keeps its line; a fixed joint none.

slide.description: LDU along an axle's, a bar's or a pin's line

to.description: the part it goes on and that part's connector: "torso.hinge[0]" (a part named so before this one) or "#41.stud[3]" (a brick standing, by its number). Types: stud, open, hole, tube, post, axle, cross, pin, socket, bar, clip, hinge, ball, fixed; numbered from 0 in each type, as attachment_points lists them

yaw.description: degrees about the joint's axis: a hinge's or a clip's angle, an arm's swing, a turn on a stud or an axle

axis.description: for a pin, an axle, a gear, a bush, a beam or a tyre put on a line: the way its axle, pin, hole or round runs. x, y and z are then where that joint's middle goes (the point attachment_points gives a hole, an axle or a rim), not the low corner, and face is not used.

face.description: which way the studs point. Omit for up.

joint.description: with axis: which of the part's own holes, pins or axles goes there, numbered as attachment_points lists them; omit for the one at its middle

name.description: a name for this part, which a later part attaches to it by: "torso" in "torso.hinge[0]"

pitch.description: and then lift its +z end, degrees. A part that leans must turn on a joint.

roll.description: and then lift its +x side, degrees

rot.description: quarter turns about the face direction, 0-3; with axis, about that line

section.description: the section this brick belongs to, if any. Its x, y and z are then that section's own coordinates, not the model's.

x.description: studs across, to the low corner. Tenths allowed.

y.description: plates up from the ground, to the low corner. Quarters allowed, for parts lying on their side.

yaw.description: turn this one part off the grid, degrees about the upright (its +z swings towards +x), about its own corner; it becomes a section of one. Any angle.

z.description: studs deep, to the low corner. Tenths allowed.

assemblies.description: name a part of the model, as submit_design's assemblies do; one of the same name moves to the new box. Something meant to stand apart from the model — a display stand, a sign, a nameplate in front of it — must be named, its box holding it and none of the model: a piece apart that nothing names is a part that has come off, and fails.

name.description: what a person would call it, e.g. north-east tower

y_from.description: may be left out, for all of its height

check_only.description: try the change without making it: says whether it would be applied, or why not and the nearest place each refused part fits and holds

repeat_section.description: say a section again somewhere else. One bay of a wall, repeated — rather than forty bays dictated.

around.description: {"x", "z"}: a centre, in the coordinates the section is built in. Each copy is carried round it by its yaw step, keeping its pitch and roll — a ring of panels round a dome.

axis.description: which way that pin runs. Defaults to the source section's.

degrees.description: turned this much further per copy, about the section's own origin. Put that origin at the centre of a tower and this walks the copies round it.

from.description: the name of a section that already has bricks in it

name.description: what to call the copies. They are numbered from 2.

times.description: how many copies to make, each one step further than the last

yaw.description: degrees further round per copy (360 / how many in the ring)

room.description: more room than the selection gives, in studs and plates, when the change cannot be made inside it. The person is asked in the app, and the change goes ahead only if they say yes.

sections.description: add a section, or give one that already exists a new angle or position — its name and only what changes — which moves everything in it and within it without naming a single brick.

axis.description: or one turn about one pin: z tips it left and right, x forward and back, y swings it round. Applied after yaw, pitch and roll.

degrees.description: how far it is turned about that axis or line. Any angle.

hinge.description: turn it on a real joint, both halves laid for you: "tilting" (or true; 3937 under 3938, rests closed), "clip" (60478's bar in 63868's clip, rests in line), "click" (44302/44301, in line, where this build's parts have it). x, y, z are then where the base stands, like any brick, turned by yaw about its first stud; the section's bricks start at 0,0,0 on the top half's studs, its nose (+z) running away from the joint's line, and pitch lifts it about that line (or roll, with the line along z). A section that leans must turn on a joint; this is the one-line way.

line.description: or the turn's axis as a direction [x, y, z], instead of axis

name.description: what to call it, e.g. port nacelle

pitch.description: then degrees its nose lifts. Yaw and pitch together face a panel any way round a dome and tip it to the curve.

within.description: the section this one is built in: x, y, z (and its hinge's base) are then that section's own coordinates, and it goes where it goes. Panels hinged on panels, a chain round a dome.

x.description: studs across, where this section's own origin sits

yaw.description: degrees about the upright: its +z (its nose) swings towards +x. Applied first.

turn.description: turn bricks where they stand, about their middle, as one: they become a section turned so, as the window's Turn, Tilt and Roll do. A part that leans this way must turn on a joint; give a section its own new angle instead.

yaw.description: degrees about the upright

why.description: why the change needs that room, in a sentence the person reads

name: edit_selection

annotations.title: Where the selection takes a part

description: Where the selected parts can take another part: every open stud, anti-stud (the hollow underneath that takes a stud), side stud, pin hole, bar and clip, grouped by the way it faces, each with the part that carries it and where it is in the coordinates edit_selection takes (a section's own, for parts laid turned), and a picture with the free ones numbered. Give part= (and color=) and it seats that part on them and tries each against the model as it stands: what comes back fits and holds, to put in edit_selection's add as it is. toward= puts first the points facing that way (out: away from the model's middle, for spikes or detail on an outer face); near= {x, y, z} those nearest a place.

color.description: its LDraw colour; the colour of the part it goes on when omitted

limit.description: how many placements of part to give; 8 when omitted

part.description: a part to seat on the open points, e.g. 49668

name: where_to_attach

description: Choose one of the three sketches made with submit_design "sketch": true. It goes on the baseplate as the massing the full design is built from, and the other two are dropped. Then design the whole model from it, and submit_design that without sketch.
name: choose_sketch

description: Look a built model over the way Brickworks' own designer does after a design stands: with no assembly, the whole model measured against real LEGO® sets of its size and kind — shapes, colours, the one-off pieces, how coarse — and what to check it for; with an assembly named in submit_design, that one close up, measured, with the parts real sets of the kind use that it has none of; with a feature (eyes, beak, wheel arches, grille), the best real set's piece for it laid by the app where it goes, with a picture, to settle with settle_feature; with surface, the surface pass — the app tiles the open stud fields, slopes the staircases (plate steps two at a time), rounds a body's hard top edges, skins its plain flanks and textures a building's plain walls on the model, to settle each with settle_surface; with creative, the creative pass — three touches proposed for this subject and the best one or two added. Call it after submit_design, then once per feature, then once per assembly, working each before the next, then surface, then creative last.

assembly.description: an assembly's name as given in submit_design; omit for the whole model

creative.description: true for the creative pass, after the surface pass

feature.description: a feature the subject is known by, as listed in submit_design's features

surface.description: true for the surface pass, once the features and assemblies have had their turns

name: review_model

description: Take everything off the baseplate and start from bare ground. Do this before building something new, or the new thing is built into the old one.
name: clear_model

description: Write what is on the baseplate to an LDraw .ldr file in this app's models, where its Open finds it and other LDraw tools can read it. A name, not a path; it will not write over a model the person saved.

name.description: the file's name, such as orthanc.ldr

name: save_model

description: Choose what the model stands on, as View, Floor does: a baseplate (studs across and deep, in eights from 8 to 192, in a colour baseplates come in), a grid floor with no plate, or none — a vehicle stands on a table, a scene on a baseplate in its ground's colour. part_of_model=true makes the baseplate a part of the model: counted, saved, step 1 of the booklet. Nothing built moves. With nothing given it says what it is now.

across.description: studs along x; 16, 32 and 48 are the square ones the LEGO Group sells

colour.description: LDraw code: 2 Green, 10 Bright Green, 288 Dark Green, 19 Tan, 28 Dark Tan, 71 Light Bluish Grey, 72 Dark Bluish Grey, 378 Sand Green, 1 Blue, 15 White, 0 Black, 7 Light Grey

deep.description: studs along z; the same as across when omitted

name: set_floor

description: The model's build steps, the order the booklet and the timeline follow, as Edit, Build steps changes them. op "list" (the default) gives them with the part numbers in each; "next" or "prev" moves bricks= a step later or earlier; "new" makes a new step of bricks=; "earlier", "later", "merge" (with the next) and "delete" act on step=, a number from the list. A model with no steps of its own is given the worked-out ones first, in the same undo step.

bricks.description: part numbers from look_at_model, for next, prev and new

from.description: list from this step; 1 when omitted

step.description: a step's number, for earlier, later, merge and delete

name: edit_steps

description: The booklet's pages as Instructions would print them now, without drawing a picture: each page with the steps on it, and for each step how its designer set it (turned, tilted, zoomed, larger or smaller, a new page or a page alone, its parts list left off), which sub-assemblies are built in a callout box and which on pages of their own, and the most steps a page. Steps the booklet turns round by itself are decided when it is drawn. Changes nothing.

from.description: list from this page; 2, the first page of steps, when omitted

name: booklet_layout

annotations.title: Set how a booklet step is printed

description: Set how the booklet prints a step, as the timeline's Booklet row and Build, Booklet page do; one undo step, saved with the model (a turn as LDraw's 0 ROTSTEP, which LPub, LDCad and Studio read). step= a number from booklet_layout or edit_steps. turn= degrees round from the usual angle and tilt= degrees higher, held for the steps after it until turned again, or turn="usual"; zoom= 0.5 to 3 (in on what the step adds); size= 0.6 to 2 on the page; page= "new", "alone" or "auto"; parts= false leaves its parts list off; sign= false leaves off the turn sign a step turned more than 60 degrees round or 45 up or down gets; callout= false builds the sub-assembly the step puts on on pages of its own; per_page= 1, 2, 4 or 0 (as they fit) for the whole booklet; highlight= false leaves the new parts unoutlined in the whole booklet. The page by hand, one undo step each and alone in a call: place= moves an item of the step's page to x, y (and w, h) in mm on the 269 x 199 page, as dragging it on Lay out the page does (item picture, parts, callout or number; note with index= for words or a picture added; remove=true takes a note off, back=true puts an item back where the booklet lays it); text= puts words on the step's page; arrow= draws an arrow on it, from x1, y1 to x2, y2, bent through bx, by if given, red (where a part goes in) or black, 0.45, 0.9 or 1.4 mm wide, or with index= changes or removes one. What is placed goes with its step when the pages change. booklet_layout says where each is, and what was moved off what it overlapped. A model with no steps of its own is given the worked-out ones first, in the same undo step.

arrow.description: {x1, y1, x2, y2, bx, by, colour, width, index, remove}: mm; colour red or black, width 0.45, 0.9 or 1.4; index= an arrow of the step's page to change, remove=true to take it off

place.description: {item, x, y, w, h, index, remove}: w and h kept when omitted

back.description: true: where the booklet lays it out again

index.description: which note, from 0, for item note

sign.description: false: no turn sign on the step

text.description: {words, x, y, w, h, size}: mm, size the letters' height (4 when omitted)

name: edit_booklet

annotations.title: Lay a hose, tube or chain

description: Lay a hose, tube, string or chain, as Build, Hose, tube or chain does: kind ribbed_hose, pneumatic_tube, flex_hose or flex_axle between two parts' pin holes, axles or pins; string between two studs; chain or tread round sprockets= (two or more gears in one plane). The real length that fits is chosen, and it bends no tighter than the real one can. It goes in as one sub-assembly, named in the answer; item= that name lays it again between new ends.

x.description: studs: the connector nearest this, when the part has several

item.description: a hose already laid, by its name in an earlier answer

sprockets.description: part numbers of the gears a chain or tread goes round

x.description: studs: the connector nearest this, when the part has several

name: lay_flex

description: Swing a part about its joint, as Build, Pose does: a sub-assembly on a hinge, a turntable or a clip on a bar. With no joint it lists them, numbered, with the angle each is at. joint= (number or name) and degrees= (from where it was built, -180 to 180) swings it as far as it has room; the answer says where it stopped if something is in the way.

joint.description: its number or name in the list

name: pose_model

annotations.title: Move a part on its joint

description: Move a part about its joint as the person's drag on it does. With no part= it changes nothing and says what moves in the model: what its link's card says (steering, a boom, doors...) with the part to take hold of, and every part on a joint. With part=, its whole rigid body and everything beyond it turn on the joint between it and what stays (a locked part, what stands on the baseplate, else the body with the most parts, or a heavier one standing on the floor): a hinge, a clip on a bar, a turntable, a pin or an axle in a round hole, a ball, a 1x1 round part on one stud. part= a part's number (look_at_model) or a sub-assembly's name. With nothing else it changes nothing and says what would move, on what, and how the model stands. degrees= turns it that far from where it is (a ball: about axis=), along= slides it that many studs along a bar or an axle; it stops where it meets the model, gears it drives turn by their teeth, a joint without friction swings down under its own weight once let go, and the answer says what moved, where its joint then stands from where it was built (twice 20° stands at 40°), and how the model stands then. A part held at both ends (a four-bar, a crank with its rod and piston, a steering's arms) moves as its loop allows, and says so where it locks. spin= lets it go turning that many degrees a second, as a flick does: a wheel, a gear train or a turntable on free bearings coasts and slows against their friction, and the answer says how far it spun and where it stopped. A model turned past its edge falls over and says how it lies, unless it stands on the baseplate's studs. to= [x, y, z] in studs instead draws the part to that point by its whole chain of joints back to what stays, each within its range. One undo step.

along.description: studs to slide along its line

axis.description: a ball's turn about this way (x y z), with degrees=

degrees.description: turn from where it is now

part.description: a part's number, or a sub-assembly's name; leave it out to list what moves

spin.description: let go turning this many degrees a second about its joint (after degrees=, if given): it coasts

to.description: a point in studs (x y z, as move_part says where a joint is): the part drawn there by its chain of joints

name: move_part

description: Animate the model: poses at moments, played smoothly between (an arm raised over two seconds and lowered again, doors opening), the model turned round once as well if asked, and rendered as an animation (a WebP, and an MP4 where ffmpeg is installed) where Render saves. keys: [{"t": seconds, "angles": {joint: degrees}}], joints by number or name from pose_model's list, or a part on its joint as move_part names it ("#14": a steering, a wheel, an arm on its pin), each in degrees from where it was built. Rendering needs the app in a window and is a job (job gives the result). The keys are kept as the model's motion "Animation" (list_motions, play_motion), which the person plays in Build, Motions…; render=false only keeps them.

angles.description: joint (number or name) -> degrees from where it was built

turntable.description: turn the model round once over it

name: animate_model

description: The model's own motions, kept in its file ("Open the doors", "Steer left and right"): each with its joints as move_part names them, their keys (seconds, and places from where the model was built: degrees turned, or studs slid), its driver, the motion it follows, and what it was last found to do: where each joint ended, or where it stopped and on what. A joint whose part is gone is said so. Then motions suggested from what moves (doors, steering, a boom, a turntable, gears, a rack), each tried for room, which define_motion keeps. Changes nothing.

suggest.description: suggest motions from what moves; true when omitted

name: list_motions

annotations.title: Keep a motion in the model

description: Keep a named motion in the model, as a builder names it ("Open the dome"), played by the real joints as a drag moves them. tracks= each a joint (a part's number "#80" or a sub-assembly's name, as move_part names them) and its keys: t= seconds, place= degrees turned from where the model was built (studs slid, with slide=true), how= ease (the default), linear or hold. Or driver= a joint turned turns= times over seconds=, from where it stands: what it drives through gears, racks and linkages follows. after= the motion it follows, for a sequence. suggested=true keeps list_motions' suggestion of that name; remove=true takes a motion out. It is saved with the model (its autosave, a save, an export, a shared link), one undo step, and answers by playing it once and putting the model back: where each joint ended, or stopped and on what.

joint.description: a crank, an axle or a gear: #N or a sub-assembly

turns.description: turns; less than 0 the other way

name.description: what a builder calls it: Open the doors

suggested.description: keep list_motions' suggestion of this name

joint.description: a part's number (#80) or a sub-assembly's name

place.description: degrees (or studs) from where it was built

slide.description: slid along its line, places in studs

name: define_motion

description: Play one of the model's motions (list_motions) through its real joints, as a drag moves them: a joint stops where it meets the model, and gears, racks and linkages follow. The model is left where the motion ends, one undo step. reverse=true plays it backwards (closes what it opened; a driver turns back), sequence=true plays the whole sequence it is in (after=), in order. The answer says where each joint ended or stopped and on what, how the model then stands, and carries a picture of its frames.
name: play_motion

description: Render one of the model's motions as an animation, a WebP and an MP4 (where ffmpeg is installed) where Render saves, framed on what it moves, without changing the model. reverse= and sequence= as play_motion; fps= 12 or 24; size= 480x300 or 720p; view= where the camera stands, hero (three-quarter from the front left, the default) or back for what moves at the back. Needs the app in a window, and is a job (job gives the result, with a picture of its frames).
name: render_motion

description: Turn the model's gear train as Tools, Simulate mechanism does, and what it drives in a loop as a drag moves it (a pinion's rack slides, a crank's rod rocks and its slider strokes), without changing the model: from driver= (a part's number or a sub-assembly's name; else the one named Crank, Motor or Handle, else the one that turns most). It says each turning part's turns per driver turn and, with reference= (the part periods are counted in; Earth when one is named so), every other's period in its turns, against the real one for a planet or targets= ({name: period}). It names a locked train's meshes and the free and floating parts by number, and weighs the balance over the whole cycle: the worst frame, the arm furthest past the base's edge, a picture of it there. record=true also renders turns= turns of the reference (1) in frames= frames (24) as a WebP and an MP4 where Render saves, as a job (job gives the result).

driver.description: a part's number from look_at_model, or a sub-assembly's name

frames.description: frames in a recording, 2 to 240; 24 when omitted

reference.description: the turning part periods are counted in: a number or a name

targets.description: name -> the period wanted, in the reference's turns

turns.description: turns of the reference (or the driver) a recording covers; 1 when omitted

name: simulate_mechanism

description: Take back the last change to the model, as Edit, Undo does — yours or the person's — or steps= of them. redo=true puts back what was undone. The answer names what was undone and what is next.
name: undo

description: The person's saved models and the examples that come with the app, with their part counts; name= opens one in place of what is on the baseplate, as File, Open does. Each save is kept as a version, the last 20, as File, Versions… shows: versions=true lists name='s, newest first, and version=N opens the Nth. link= a gallery model's link id (gallery) opens a copy of it saved in the person's models, as Open in Brickworks on its page does. Opening cannot be undone, so it is refused while the model has changes not saved, unless discard_changes=true.

link.description: a gallery model's link id, or its /m/ address

name.description: a model's name from the list

version.description: open this save of name=, 1 the newest

versions.description: list name='s saves kept as versions

name: open_model

description: The model's parts, as Build, Parts list shows them: by part and colour, with counts and LEGO® element ids. which="need" measures it against the person's collection (My collection): how much they own and what they are short of; which="buildable" is What can I build?: their saved models, the examples and the official models of real sets, ranked by how much of each they own.
name: parts_list

description: Render the model as File, Render does: a picture, or a turntable (a WebP and, where ffmpeg is installed, an MP4), on a studio sweep with soft shadows. quality quick, good or best (good for a picture, quick for a turntable when omitted); size 720p, 1080p, 4k or square; view hero, front, side, back, low or top. Saved where Render saves. It is a job: the answer is a job number at once, and job gives the result, a picture with it. Needs the app in a window.
name: render_model

description: Write the model out as File, Export does, where Export writes (the Downloads folder; a download on the web): format ldraw (.ldr, or .mpd with its sub-models, with its build steps), studio (a BrickLink Studio .io), a 3D file at real size — glb (one file: Blender, three.js, AR; any size of model), gltf (the same as text), obj (with an .mtl of its colours) or stl (one mesh in mm, Z up, to 3D print); obj and stl hold every triangle and are capped — picture (.png), bricklink (a wanted list), rebrickable (a parts list .csv), or instructions (the building instructions as a booklet to print); all_models is every model the person saved, as LDraw in one .zip (File, Export, All my models). studio, picture and instructions are jobs: the answer is a job number at once, and job gives the result.
name: export_model

description: Lay a 3D model in LEGO® bricks, as Build, Brickify a 3D model… does: an OBJ, STL, glTF/GLB, PLY, 3MF, VOX or FBX laid at the size asked (studs along its longest side) in slopes, curves and tiles, or plain bricks and plates, as one sub-assembly named after the file, beside what is built. file= its path on this computer (the desktop app), or url= an http(s) link to the file, fetched by the app (96 MB at most; an OBJ's .mtl and a .gltf's .bin come from beside it). pick=true opens the window's file dialog for the person to choose one on their computer, and says so; once they have, brickify with neither lays what the panel shows. Laying is a job: the answer is a job number, and job gives the result: whether it is one piece and stands (weighed), on what, any stand it was given, what was joined, and anything left out, where and why; its steps, a course a step with every step's build standing; and how to get its booklet and lists. collection=true lays it from the person's collection: their parts and colours first, then stand-ins, the shortfall said.

collection.description: lay it from the person's collection (My collection)

colours.description: its own, all colour=, or its own cut to the limit= it uses most

file.description: the path of an .obj, .stl, .gltf, .glb, .ply, .3mf, .vox or .fbx on this computer

limit.description: how many colours, for colours limit

pick.description: open the file dialog for the person

smooth.description: slopes, curves, tiles and studs sideways; true when omitted

stand.description: a stand under it where it would tip or stands on legs or wheels much thinner than itself; true when omitted

studs.description: studs along its longest side, 6 to 64; 24 when omitted

up.description: which of the file's axes is up; a printer's STL is +Z

name: brickify

description: Print a picture on a part of the model, or stick it on as a sticker, as Build, Print on a part… and Put a sticker on… do. brick= the part's number in look_at_model. A print goes on one of the part's printable areas (area=, the first when omitted; a wrong one is answered with its areas), and the printed part takes the part's place in its colour, a part of its own from then on. sticker=true makes a sticker the size of the part's side= face (up, down, +x, -x, +z, -z), running over the faces in the same plane beside it unless span=false, and sticks it on. The picture: svg= drawn by you (a whole <svg> with a viewBox in the face's proportions; flat colours print best), picture_data= a picture's own bytes as base64 or a data: URI (a PNG or JPEG the person gave you in the conversation; at most 2 MB, smaller is quicker), or picture_url= an http(s) link to a PNG, JPEG, WebP or SVG. Or the LEGO Group's own, as Edit, Printed versions… does: version= one of the part's printed or stickered versions from the library (versions="words" lists them) swaps the part for it where it stands; sticker_part= a sticker the library has (search_parts "sticker") sticks it on the side= face, lying on it.

colour.description: the film's LDraw colour for sticker_part; white (15) when omitted

name.description: what the print or sticker is called

picture_data.description: the picture's bytes as base64, or a data:image/…;base64, URI

sticker_part.description: a sticker from the library, by id, to stick on the side= face

version.description: a printed or stickered version of the part, by id, to swap it for

versions.description: list the part's printed versions with these words in their names; "" for all

name: print_part

description: Cut one copy of a sub-assembly loose from the others, as Edit, Make this copy unique does: it becomes a sub-assembly of its own, so changing it changes no other copy. assembly= its path or name ("Wheel#2" or "Wheel (copy 2)"), or brick= a part in it.

brick.description: a part in the copy, by its number

name: make_unique

description: Colour the parts nobody sees in the finished model, as big sets are coloured inside so a builder can tell where they are, as Tools, Colour the hidden parts… does. Hidden is measured, never guessed: the model drawn from 128 sides, every part its own colour, and only parts seen from none of them change. mode: sections (the booklet's: the assemblies a design named), stages (the build cut into stages= stages, as bags are), left_right or front_back (the halves of a symmetrical build told apart). Each group gets one colour far from every colour seen, and each part only a colour it is made in. Without apply it changes nothing and shows the inside cut open, coloured. Offer it at the end of a big model built in sections, never by default: apply=true with agreed=true only once the person has said yes; a model from a real set also needs set_agreed=true. One step to undo; the booklet shows each colour where its group starts.

agreed.description: the person said yes to this

from_below.description: true when omitted: a part seen from underneath keeps its colour. false for a display model never turned over

set_agreed.description: the person said yes to recolouring a real set's own parts

stages.description: for stages: how many, 2 to 12; two when omitted, as most real sets use one or two

name: colour_hidden_parts

description: How a builder would split the model into sections, as Build, Suggest sections does: the way a set splits into numbered bags and sub-builds. Each is connected and one piece, of a sensible size, joined to the rest by few joints, numbered in the order it is built, with the sections it is built onto and the way it comes off. Read from the booklet planner and the build check's joint graph. Changes nothing in the model; the suggestion is shown in the person's model tree. make_sections makes them sub-assemblies.
name: suggest_sections

description: Make the suggested sections (suggest_sections) sub-assemblies, as one undo step, as the model tree's Accept all does. With no sections= every suggestion as suggested; with sections= one sub-assembly for each entry: its name and the numbers of the suggestions it is made of (two or more merge them). Parts already in a sub-assembly go inside the new one.
name: make_sections

description: Pull a section (a sub-assembly) away from the model the way it comes off, as Build, Break out the section does: up off the studs it stands on, or out to the side it is joined on, clear of the rest by two studs, by whole studs and bricks. One undo step. Work on it there with edit_model as anywhere. put_back=true puts it exactly where it was (one undo step); all=true puts every section back. Saved and exported files always have every section in place.

section.description: its name or path, as the sub-assemblies are listed

name: break_out_section

description: A section on its own, as Build, Evaluate the section does: its parts and count, its parts list, weight, whether it holds together as a separate build (the build check on it alone), whether it stands on its own base (Balance), what joins it to the rest and whether those joints carry its load, and how many steps it takes alone. section= a sub-assembly's name or path, or suggestion= a suggest_sections number. Changes nothing.
name: evaluate_section

description: Search brickworks.diy/gallery, the models people built in Brickworks and shared, and open one as a reference. With no open: a page of models matching q (words of a name, a builder, a tag or a description), kind, size, technic, instructions, sorted by sort (top: Top builds; owned: Parts I own, signed in with a collection); each with its link id, part count, credit, licence, how many built it and what moves in it (steering, a boom: anybody can move them on its link). shelves=true: the gallery's front, this week's pick and the small builds, and what the person can build now from their collection. open=<id>: one model compactly — what it is, its size, its sub-assemblies and steps, its parts by kind and the most used, its credit and its licence, how many built it, its comments and photos of real builds, and its picture — to learn how it is built. designer=<handle> (a list's "by Name (@handle)"): a designer's page, what their models earned and their models. Read-only: nothing on the baseplate changes, and liking, following and commenting are the person's own, on the site. Credit its builder and keep to its licence in anything made from it.

designer.description: a designer's handle, from a list's "by Name (@handle)"

instructions.description: only models with their builder's own steps

open.description: a model's link id, from a search, to read it

picture.description: with open: its picture too; true when omitted

q.description: words to look for, up to 100 characters

shelves.description: the gallery's front: this week's pick, the small builds, and what the person can build now

sort.description: newest when omitted; owned only for a person signed in with a collection

name: gallery

description: How a long piece of work is going: a call that answered with a job number (a render, a turntable, a booklet, a Studio file, a Brick Art picture, a brickify, a mechanism's recording, or any call still going after 20 s). It waits up to 10 s for the work to end, then says how far it has got; once done it gives the work's answer, picture and all, or why it stopped. cancel=true stops it, as Cancel in the window does. id= the job's number; the latest when omitted.

cancel.description: stop it, where it can be stopped

id.description: the number the call answered with

name: job
